_why: This guard exists because the failure it catches is INVISIBLE: the write succeeds and the overflow is dropped at LOAD time, so nothing in the tree looks wrong. That shape makes the whole battery vulnerable to a mutation that simply reports OK — which is why the loosening mutations dominate here. The load-bearing row is `byte-only-check-ignores-the-line-cap`: it is the obvious simplification of this script, it leaves every byte test passing, and only the worst-dimension tests can see it. Each mutation names the ONE test it is aimed at, so a kill by an unrelated assertion, a crash or a timeout is reported as a survivor with the real catcher named.

mutations.name: byte-only-check-ignores-the-line-cap
mutations._mechanism: THE simplification a future author reaches for: score bytes and stop. An index at 40% of its byte cap and 105% of its line cap then reports OK while its tail is being dropped. Every byte-dimension test still passes, so only the worst-dimension battery can see it.

mutations.name: over-becomes-greater-or-equal
mutations._mechanism: Off-by-one against the loader, which tests `size > cap`. An index sitting EXACTLY at the cap would be reported OVER and sent for a compaction it does not need — the false-positive direction, which erodes trust in the guard until someone stops running it.

mutations.name: warn-threshold-becomes-strictly-greater
mutations._mechanism: An index landing exactly on 80% reports OK. The boundary is the one value a threshold is most likely to be tested at and most likely to be got wrong.
mutations.find: "OVER" if worst["over"] else "WARN" if worst["frac"] >= WARN_FRAC else "OK"
mutations.replace: "OVER" if worst["over"] else "WARN" if worst["frac"] > WARN_FRAC else "OK"

mutations.name: warn-no-longer-sets-the-exit-code
mutations._mechanism: WARN still PRINTS, so a human reading stdout sees it, but the CLI exits 0 and every gate built on it passes. WARN is the actionable state — it is the last moment compaction is cheap — so silencing it defers every index to OVER, where content is already lost.

mutations.name: unreadable-index-reports-ok
mutations._mechanism: `I could not read it` collapsing into `it is fine` — the asymmetry this repo already enforces for the worktree comment and the state-file search. An index that has been moved or corrupted would exit 0.
mutations.find:
except OSError as exc:
        return ("UNREADABLE", f"UNREADABLE {path} ({exc})")
mutations.replace:
except OSError:
        return ("OK", "OK unreadable treated as fine")

mutations.name: dropped-text-measured-from-the-wrong-end
mutations._mechanism: Returns the HEAD instead of the TAIL. The count stays right, so `dropped=254` still reads correctly, and the operator is shown 254 bytes of text that is perfectly visible while the entries actually being lost stay hidden. A count-only assertion cannot see this.
mutations.find: return raw[byte_cap:].decode("utf-8", "replace") if len(raw) > byte_cap else ""
mutations.replace: return raw[:byte_cap].decode("utf-8", "replace") if len(raw) > byte_cap else ""

mutations.name: inode-dedup-collapses-distinct-indexes
mutations._mechanism: A de-dup keyed on something every file shares reports ONE index no matter how many exist, hiding every index but the first. It passes the hardlink test — which is why that test needed a distinct-files sibling.

mutations.name: line-count-drops-the-unterminated-final-line
mutations._mechanism: `wc -l` semantics: count newlines. An index whose last line has no trailing newline is then under-counted by one, and an index sitting exactly at the line cap reads as under it. The off-by-one is invisible on any fixture that happens to end with a newline, which is most of them.

mutations.name: compaction-target-uses-the-warn-fraction
mutations._mechanism: Targets 80% instead of 70%, so a compaction done to this script's own advice lands just under the warn line and re-warns almost immediately. The number is advice, not a gate, which is exactly why nobody would notice it drifting.

mutations.name: kb-rendering-switches-to-decimal-kb
mutations._mechanism: 25000/1000 renders '25.0KB' where the hook says '24.4KB'. The script and the built-in warning would then disagree about the same number, and a reader reconciling them concludes one of the two is measuring something else.
